body.text: Work is not what it was. Does the office even still exist or has it been replaced by teams that could be anywhere? In republishing Moya Costello’s short novel The Office as a Boat a quarter of a century after its first appearance, Pink Shorts Press has been perspicacious. The book shows how much the world has changed, locally, specifically, and how fast. Almost everything will be recognisable to those who remember work in that earlier time. It also recalls the period before the office became a destination, especially for women, creating another shadow further back in time.

Costello’s office “as a boat” circa 1990s is open plan, horizontal rather than vertical, consultative by design. It is populated by a group of sharply individuated female “communication workers” and an upper echelon of a few useless men. Yet what looks like freeing turns out to be enslaving too.

In this satirically fictional office the women brighten their day with idiosyncrasies that carry over from their private lives. This is a time when the uptake of new technology is required and largely welcome. They produce material for publication, adapting their skills with computer and screen as the digital inexorably takes over. Windows provide a pervasive metaphor, always framing, opening but delimiting. It seems like old technology now, which is part of the book’s charm as well as what makes it scary. How quickly things, including people, are discarded.
Do you remember the importance of stationery in the workplace of yesteryear? It was a carefully guarded, fetishistic matter. Who got what? Here’s a sample from the order book in The Office as a Boat:

a stapler for Casey, Post-it notes for Verity, a hole puncher for Nell, white-out for Lou, a pencil sharpener for Audrey, an eraser for Susan, and envelopes for Sarah. I liked to order esoteric items like a staple remover and a rubber thimblette.
Droll observance is the narrator’s way of coping. These days we go to Officeworks, if we need such things at all.

Then there’s flexitime and the diabolical sheets required to manage it. They were advance warning of what would happen with Work From Home, accelerated by online shopping and the pandemic. Do Everything from Home. If you can. Don’t Go Out. For an earlier generation of women, work was a fought-for right as well as an aspiration. Getting out of the house was a way of contributing to society on equal terms with men, or better. Yet it didn’t always deliver, as Costello wryly shows. “I’d left full-time work and turned down another job to do voluntary work I’d always wanted to do,” her narrator says. “But by then the economy had permanently changed.” Neoliberalism was in full swing. In a list of options for her life she had written “Get a career,” imagining there would be a way to balance having enough money to live on and enough time to pursue her own interests. That dream turned into “a job in an office.”

In the office you have to leave your dreaming behind, and live in the front of your head where all the analysis is done, where the facts of history, accepted as such, are plotted, where logic operates, where emotion is scantily represented.

Among the women themselves there are countervailing interactions that persist as a revenant of the socialist feminist collective, resisting the managerialist male order. But as the narrator says, “A woman had to be a monk, not to be caught up in the whirl of office activity and talk.”

Accessories and accoutrements are vividly registered — mugs, flowers, clothes, garden produce, pets, faces open and closed. The city is going through a drought. The narrator’s commute is along one of the arterial roads that “were forever attached to Adelaide’s city centre, leading immutably in and out, straight and flat, offering no variation or flexibility,” like the office: “this artificial creation, this illusion of order within boundaries and purposeful activity with limited scope.”

It’s laugh-out-loud bleakness through the lens of someone whose “growing-up place” was elsewhere, on the watery Parramatta River. With her insider/outsider perspective, no one has written better about Adelaide than Moya Costello.

The Office as a Boat. Not is a boat. You have to say the title twice to get it right. The plot is wild. The writing is free as a bird. Weird, considered. From a writer who is not a household name nor a literary prize winner, but who was active in the field for more than forty years, it’s puzzling and emancipatory.

A back story to the book might be Moya Costello’s own trajectory. Born in 1952, she was part of the underground, feminist, small magazine and independent publishing scene that had an epicentre in Glebe, Sydney, in the 1970s and ’80s. There was a commitment to collective work and activism and no one was paid much. Reminiscing about Glebe in those days, Anna Couani mentions the Sydney Women Writers Workshop she helped found, listing the many who “went on to become well-known writers and activists: Susan Hampton, Joanne Burns, Pam Brown, Chris Mansell, Dorothy Johnson, Inez Baranay, Mary Fallon, Jill Jones, Jenni Nixon, Caroline Gerrish, Sarah St Vincent Welch, Barbara Brooks, Moya Costello, Jane Skelton, Virginia Shepherd, Gina Mercer, Sue Kucharova, Marion Consandine, Coren Caplan, Anna Valerio, Loretta Re, Jo Garolis, Annee Lawrence, Chitra Fernando, Beatriz Copello, Lee Cataldi, Carmel Kelly, Sal Brereton, Erica Callan – the list goes on….”

It was always political. Moya (let me call her from here on) and her life partner Jeff Williams were environmental activists in Sydney in 1979. They put together the newsletter for the Movement Against Uranium Mining using the layout of Tribune, the Communist Party of Australia newspaper. Moya wrote for it. The “experimental writing” she advocated as a creative writer was never meant to be inaccessible. She believed in alternative ways of doing things. She liked to push the boundaries of her various writing communities.

The couple moved to Melbourne in 1981 and Moya worked for a while as an usherette. Her first book, Kites in Jakarta, includes “The Usherette” among other short pieces of creative prose and was published by Anna Couani’s Sea Cruise Press in 1985, in a double bill with Carmel Kelly’s The Waters of Vanuatu. By then Moya had moved with Jeff to Adelaide. Small Ecstasies, a second book of short semi-fictional prose, was published by UQP in 1994 and marked a literary arrival of sorts.

But Moya preferred more precarious publishing. The Office as a Boat was first published by Brandl & Schlesinger in 2000, then Harriet Chandler, a novel-length work, under her own imprint, Short Odds Publishing, in 2014. She describes it as a “hybrid text”: the “fictional biography” of a character who first appeared in Murray Bail’s 1987 novel Holden’s Performance. That made it pretty much unclassifiable. Moya’s last published book was pressed specimens, published by Beir Bua Press (Ireland) in 2022, consisting of prose poems inspired by the Medicinal Plant Herbarium, Southern Cross University, where she taught from 2008–17 after moving to the Northern Rivers.

Moya was always inventive. She could be zany, sometimes a refusenik, but never a careerist in her choices. Her work in mentoring others mostly came first. She was interested in all aspects of the making of writing and staunchly supported independent publishing. Her first-person narrator in The Office as a Boat writes:

The use of desktop publishing technology, the blurring of roles between publisher, typesetter, editor, writer and graphic artist, enabled one person, using a morphing methodology, to be many things and become a kind of magician, an alchemist of publishing, as much earlier in the industry: Baskerville had made his own paper, blended his inks and cut a typeface.

In real life Moya’s father, Frank Costello, had worked in the stationery and printing area of a NSW government department and she was aware of that legacy. Her narrator also knows that the utopian possibilities of a new era of electronic communication are already being coopted for consumerist corporate purposes.

The tributes to Moya Costello from her former students have flowed since her death in 2025. “She taught the intangible,” writes one. An issue of Coastlines Journal has been dedicated to her, including a fine commemoration by Lynda Hawryluk, her colleague at Southern Cross, where she continued as an adjunct after moving to Tasmania with Jeff.

Pink Shorts’s edition of The Office as a Boat includes an introduction by Holly Gramazio, who was one of Moya’s students at the University of Adelaide. Holly is now a London-based game designer whose first novel, The Husbands, was a New York Times bestseller in 2024. Moya supported her through a complicated PhD in Creative Writing. The project was a crossword puzzle based on the city grid of Adelaide, with a story from a twenty-four-hour narrative that generated each clue. Sound complicated? It required a willing embrace of new technology. Looking back on Moya’s career, Holly observes: “When someone does so much, so many different things, I think it can be harder to make sense of who they are and the shape of their work.”

Part of the point is that Moya was classified as general staff at Adelaide at the time, not academic staff, meaning she came there by a different path and had different skills. The demarcation line was less rigid then. She worked in the Humanities office with six or seven co-workers. Hard to imagine that these days, when the institution itself has flipped its name — to Adelaide University. The gig economy has changed work there too: fractional positions, unpaid internships, precarity. Out of a job with a PhD in mid-life, a lollypop person for night roadworks gets better money. Stop, Slow.

I was the incoming chair of creative writing in 2005, back in the academy after twenty years and on a steep learning curve. Moya produced the handbook for the PhD in Creative Writing, which became influential around the country as the degree spread. She had the lingo and the desktop and online publishing experience. She was equally committed to creative writing outside the academy and instrumental in arguing that public readings should be valued as a form of dissemination. She had a high regard for the Lee Marvin Readings curated by poet Ken Bolton for the Experimental Art Foundation. Ken, who moved to Adelaide in 1982, was another refugee from the Sydney “Tin Sheds” scene.

Moya returned for a guest appearance at Ken’s readings a few years ago, wearing the tutu that features in The Office as a Boat: “I bought a black leather jacket and wore it to the office with the tutu. I had my hair cut grimly short,” the narrator writes. She travels by bus. “All passengers want to surround themselves with an invisible shield that they hope will protect them from contact with others.” Here, characteristically, the prose balloons from quirky particular to larger empathy.

Among those Moya mentored I count myself, with lasting gratitude. Being a writer and teaching creative writing are not always compatible. When I took the job in 2005, I was sick of fiction, even though my most recent novel, Original Face, had been named one of the books of the year. I was ready to lie fallow for ten years. But Moya goaded me.

A project called 1001 Nights Cast had been conceived by artist/activist Barbara Campbell in which a phrase from media coverage of events in the Middle East was sent to a designated story writer who had to write a 1001-word story incorporating that phrase and have it ready to be read aloud and broadcast online by sunset the same day. Moya said she would accept the challenge if I would. The result for me was a series of short pieces which I then read myself at Lee Marvin when I was invited. I included them in Bapo, a collection of my fiction that came out in 2014. A review said they were “make-weight” pieces, but I think they are some of the best things I’ve done. They got me going in a new direction. One was used as a translation exercise by students in China. I don’t know that it helped the conflict in the Middle East though.

I spoke at the memorial celebration for Moya Costello at Port Sorrel in Tasmania where she lived in her last years. People attended online from the various writing communities Moya had nurtured. There were lots of people in person from local community groups in which she participated, including a writing group in nearby Deloraine represented by an emerging writer of historical fiction and her daughter, who joined the group aged six and drew a leopard at Moya’s suggestion.

The invisible and the intangible can be what a good mentor leaves behind, in which lives are changed. That happened many times in Moya’s case. Beyond the hot picks of the season there is another version of writing in Australia that goes steadily on — through blogs, local bookstores, live readings, writing workshops, small publications and big readers: the grassroots where literature lives. Think of ANZ LitLovers and reviewer Lisa Hill. Or whisperinggums.com, nationwide. Or the readings that have replaced Lee Marvin in Adelaide now Ken Bolton has retired. Although writers never retire.

It remains personal, like Moya’s peculiar obsession with Murray Bail, which extended to Helen Garner, the artist Ian Fairweather and more, in fugitive essays such as “Abu Ben Bail: A Creative Writer Reads Murray Bail’s Archived Correspondence” (2017), “Myth-archetype-story-f[r]iction: Helen Garner’s How to End a Story” (2022) and “little jokes that nobody but me will understand” (2023). She was a fan.

A raft of such uncollected writings by Moya Costello is there to treasure and archive. Much is generously available on open access. Some is unpublished. The Office as a Boat has found its moment. It joins a significant group of Australian novels about work that include Dorothy Hewett’s Bobbin’ Up (1959), David Ireland’s The Unknown Industrial Prisoner (1971) and Frank Moorhouse’s Edith Trilogy (1993–2011). It may reference Jane Austen, but it sits equally with the brilliant one-off short novels by mid-twentieth-century New York women writers, such as Jane Bowles’s Two Serious Ladies (1943) and Elizabeth Hardwick’s Sleepless Nights (1979).

Set during a heatwave and ending as the flood waters rise, The Office as a Boat is prophetic in its foreboding. The airconditioned office no longer holds. Yet there’s a hilarious, surreal liberation that balances the clear-eyed apprehension. The morning that opens the book is “like the morning of a holy day.” The event that concludes it is nothing short of miraculous. That’s why this strange, brilliant book can truly be called a joy. •
